analysis.one_liner: Opens all federal land, including national parks, to natural gas pipelines with fast-track permits.
analysis.headline: The House Natural Resources Committee approved the bill 21-15 and placed it on the floor calendar in October 2015, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Mineral Leasing Act to allow natural gas pipelines on every type of federally owned land, including national parks, except tribal trust lands and offshore areas. It would require the Interior Department to designate at least 10 pipeline "corridors" within two years, lock them into federal land-use plans, approve rights-of-way within one year, and skip the normal environmental review for the corridor designations themselves. The bill cleared committee but never came up for a vote on the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Natural gas pipeline companies gain guaranteed routes across federal land, a one-year permit deadline, and an exemption from environmental review for the corridor designations themselves. Natural gas producers gain expanded pipeline capacity to move gas to market, which could modestly lower prices for consumers.

how_it_helps.text: Opens natural gas pipeline rights-of-way on all federally owned land, including the National Park System, except tribal trust lands and the Outer Continental Shelf.
Requires the Interior Department to designate at least 10 energy corridors within two years and fold them into federal land-use plans, and lets state governors request corridors.
Requires approval of pipeline rights-of-way in corridors within one year, with a predictable timeline given to applicants up front.
Declares that corridor designations are not "major federal actions" under the National Environmental Policy Act, so no environmental impact statement is required for the designation itself.
The committee amendment added that individual rights-of-way applications must still meet the environmental protections in the existing Mineral Leasing Act process.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on everyone who uses national parks and other federal lands, which could host permanent pipeline corridors with no limit on their number or length, and on communities near the routes. The public would also lose the environmental review normally required before these designations are locked into land-use plans.

drawbacks.text: The bill places no limit on the number or physical length of corridors the Interior Secretary may designate.
Corridor designations are exempt from environmental impact review under NEPA, so the decisions locking pipelines into land-use plans happen without that analysis.
Pipelines could cross National Park System lands, which current law generally does not allow.

A fair-faith supporter's case — that more pipelines could improve reliability and lower natural gas prices — rests on the bill's own stated goals, not on analysis the bill requires; meanwhile the expedited one-year approval timeline compresses review even for the individual applications that remain subject to environmental protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The possible consumer benefit — somewhat cheaper natural gas and better reliability — is modest and uncertain. The cost is concrete and permanent: pipeline corridors across national parks and other federal lands, locked into land-use plans without environmental review for the designation itself, with no cap on how many corridors can be created. The committee's amendment preserved environmental review for individual pipeline applications, which blunts but does not remove the concern.

outcome.mechanism: The House Natural Resources Committee approved it on a 21-15 vote and placed it on the House floor calendar in October 2015, but no floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Introduced May 13, 2015 by Rep. Tom MacArthur and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
On June 11, 2015, the committee ordered the bill reported as amended on a 21-15 vote.

The committee reported the bill on October 6, 2015 (H. Rept. 114-285) with an amendment adding environmental protections for individual rights-of-way applications, and it was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 217), the list of bills awaiting a House floor vote.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a House floor vote and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, national parks and other federal lands kept their existing protections against pipeline rights-of-way, and pipeline developers did not get the guaranteed corridors and one-year permit deadlines the bill would have provided. Consumers did not get any of the promised gas-price relief either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal lands kept existing pipeline protections

for.what_they_did: Voted to order the bill reported to the House, amended, on a 21-15 vote.

sides.party_line_note: 13 of the bill's 14 cosponsors were Republicans; the one Democrat was Rep. Cedric Richmond of Louisiana, and the committee reported it on a 21-15 vote in a Republican-majority committee.

industries.note: The bill gives pipeline builders guaranteed corridors across federal land including national parks, a one-year permit deadline, and no environmental review of the corridor designations themselves. The gain comes at the expense of public lands and the review process ordinary people rely on.

New pipeline capacity opens markets for gas producers and could lower prices for consumers, but the routes are carved through public lands with reduced review. The benefit and the burden fall on different groups.

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation and tourism businesses near parks
industries.note: Pipeline corridors across National Park System lands would degrade scenery and visitor experience that gateway businesses and their customers depend on. These businesses lose alongside the public.
